L20: # Bitcoin-Anchored Temporal Proof for Transparency Services
L21: ## 【0†Abstract】
L22: 
L23: This document defines a mechanism for temporal anchoring of digital artifacts by committing cryptographic hashes to the Bitcoin blockchain via the OpenTimestamps protocol. The resulting proof is independently verifiable by any party with access to independently validated Bitcoin chain data, without contacting the anchoring service. The SCITT Architecture is used as the primary integration example. No changes to the SCITT architecture are required.【1†¶】

L1737:   * Umarise Core API: the anchoring service, in the two deployments described above. Artifact hashes are blinded before aggregation. Origin records and proofs are held per artifact. The first deployment additionally runs the scheduled verification audit described above. No RFC 3161 timestamp is issued alongside an Anchor Proof by either deployment.【663†¶】
L1738:   * verify-anchoring.org: fully client-side verification tool. No API contact, no account, no tracking. It implements the header-only procedure of Section 3.1 in its own code, including the parsing of the proof and the comparison between the replayed digest and the Merkle root of the attested block header. Block headers are obtained from a public block explorer.
L1739: In its default configuration the tool relies on that explorer for the header and for the confirmation count, and so establishes neither the header nor the depth in the sense Section 3.1, steps 7b and 9, require. Public domain.【664†¶】
L1740:   * @umarise/cli: Node.js CLI for automated anchoring. Published on npm.【665†¶】
L1741:   * anchor-action: GitHub Actions integration for CI/CD pipeline anchoring. Published on GitHub Marketplace.【666†¶】
L1742: The two deployments now differ, and the difference is not one of degree. The first advances a proof's status from pending to anchored on the presence of a Bitcoin attestation in the upgraded proof, and on nothing further. In the terms of Section 2.6.5 it sets the producer status from the proof state alone, without establishing the confirmation state that the status is defined to record.
L1743: It does not retrieve the block header at the attested height, and so does not compare the replayed digest against the Merkle root of that header (【261†Section 4.2】, step 2e) before advancing the status, nor record that header's nTime as block_time (step 2g), nor evaluate confirmation depth (Section 3.1, step 9; step 2f). The great majority of the anchors in existence were produced by it.【667†¶】
L1744: The second deployment adopted the outstanding steps in August 2026. It validates each block header locally before verification is permitted to rely on it: the header is checked for proof-of-work against the target claimed by its own nBits field, for correct difficulty-retarget arithmetic, and for hash linkage back to a pinned checkpoint on a retarget boundary, before it is persisted.
L1745: Public block explorers remain the transport for raw header bytes; they are not relied upon to establish that a header lies on the chain. The replayed digest is compared against the Merkle root of the validated header, the header's nTime is recorded as block_time, and confirmation depth is counted against the locally validated tip rather than against a height reported by a third party.【668†¶】
L1746: What this means for conformance. Section 3.1 and 【199†Section 7.11】 state that a producing implementation SHOULD NOT promote a proof before the attested block has reached MIN_CONFIRMATIONS, and 【261†Section 4.2】 step 2f illustrates a construction that meets this. The second deployment enforces it; the first does not, and to that extent does not meet the requirement. This profile retains it rather than relaxing it, and makes no forecast of when that state will change.
L1758: Independent implementation. An implementation of the producing side of this profile, together with a verifier implementing the eleven steps of Section 3.1, was written by Tiago Pinto from the published text of this profile and the OpenTimestamps release pinned in 【198†Section 6.2.1】, without guidance from the author.
L1759: That condition was proposed by the implementer and accepted by the author: where the document could not be resolved without asking, the ambiguity was to be recorded as a defect rather than resolved by asking, and the defect report below is what that produced. Given the artifact hashes and blinding nonces of 【675†Appendix D.1】, its aggregation records, for the first vector, an operation sequence identical to the first six operations of the corresponding proof in 【676†Appendix D.5】.
L1760: The cross-checks close in both directions: that implementation returns `valid` for the proofs of 【318†Appendix D】, and the OpenTimestamps reference client verifies a proof it produced. It anchored one artifact of its own and advanced that proof to anchored only after comparing the replayed digest against the Merkle root of the header at the attested height, obtained from a Bitcoin full node under its own control, and establishing at least six confirmations.
L1761: That is the gate the first deployment does not evaluate, and which the second evaluates against a header chain it validates itself rather than against a node of its own. The package, its construction record and its defect report are published at https://donttrustverify.pt/interop/fassbender-scitt-time-anchor-03/, and that defect report is the origin of the clarification made to Section 1.4 and to 【261†Section 4.2】, step 2b in an earlier revision.【677†¶】
L1762: Independent verification of a deployed proof. On 27 August 2026 that same implementer verified, against a Bitcoin full node under his own control, one proof produced by the second deployment after it had adopted the steps described above. The replayed digest was compared with the Merkle root of the header at the attested height as that node reports it, and the comparison was performed in the implementer's own code rather than delegated to a library.
L1763: The replay and the confirmation-depth check succeeded at 833 confirmations. Steps 1 and 2 were not evaluated: what was transmitted was the commitment rather than the artifact, so the run did not return `valid` in the sense of Section 3.1, and what it establishes is that the registered hash existed no later than the attested block, not which artifact, if any, produced it. The run is recorded in a log whose SHA-256 was published before the log itself was released, and which is itself anchored.【678†¶】
L1764: Note on the defect report. A second reader arrived independently at the same resolution of that defect, from the published text alone and without consultation with the author or with that implementer. That reader operates an anchoring deployment of his own. It does not implement this profile, its leaf and receipt structures differ, and nothing here presents it as an implementation of this profile or as evidence of interoperability.
L1765: What is recorded is the concurrence on the reading, and nothing further.【679†¶】
L1766: Note on availability. The continued availability of any particular deployment depends on its hosting arrangements. The verification guarantees of this profile require no anchoring service to remain reachable: an `.ots` proof is self-contained relative to the Bitcoin blockchain, and a holder of the proof and the artifact needs nothing else.【680†¶】
L2094: The authors thank Tiago Pinto for an independent implementation of the producing side of this profile, built from the published document without consultation, and for the defect report that occasioned the clarifications in Section 1.4 and in 【261†Section 4.2】, step 2b.【722†¶】

L37: Revocation is often treated as a property of a credential, token, session, grant, policy, or identity record. In consequence-bearing systems, however, an authorization can be completely legitimate when issued and still become unsafe before the authorized operation becomes externally effective. The security question is therefore not only whether revocation exists, but whether a revocation that becomes authoritative before a protected commit is guaranteed to control that commit.
L38: The severity is deployment- dependent, but can be high in financial, administrative, AI-agent, cloud-control, confidential-compute, device, industrial, or other environments where a stale-but-valid authorization can produce an irreversible or externally consequential effect.【14†¶】
L39: This document describes a finality-bound revocation model. A Candidate Act remains in a Non-Effective State after upstream authorization. The authorization is bound to an act-specific revocation basis, such as a protected revocation generation, epoch, status root, or equivalent authority state. Immediately before the protected consequence is committed, a Finality Sink verifies that no applicable revocation, suspension, narrowing, or superseding authorization state has become load-bearing.
L40: Where the revocation state changed, the act is rejected, re-authorized, or explicitly shown to survive the change under an authoritative rule. With authoritative current state, atomic check-and-commit semantics, and complete mediation of all effectuation paths, this is intended as a prevention property for the protected stale act; deployments that permit bounded staleness or incomplete path coverage obtain mitigation rather than the same prevention guarantee.【15†¶】
L41: The model complements existing mechanisms rather than replacing them.
L42: OAuth Token Revocation [【16†RFC7009】] and Token Introspection [【17†RFC7662】] provide standardized token-state mechanisms; Microsoft Entra Continuous Access Evaluation [【18†MS-CAE】] demonstrates event-driven rejection of otherwise unexpired tokens; Amazon Verified Permissions and Cedar [【19†AWS-VERIFIED-PERMISSIONS】] provide fine-grained policy-evaluation mechanisms; Google Cloud IAM [【20†GOOGLE-IAM-DENY】] provides centrally managed deny-policy controls; and confidential-computing and attestation platforms such as NVIDIA attestation [【21†NVIDIA-ATTEST】] and Arm CCA [【22†ARM-CCA】] can provide protected execution and trust inputs.

L312: The principal threat is not limited to stolen credentials, forged tokens, or expired authorization. The difficult case is a credential or permit that is authentic, unexpired, correctly sender-constrained where applicable, and legitimately held by the same principal that was authorized earlier.【291†¶】

L325: 
L326: If the sink checks only the earlier signature, expiry, or possession proof, the act can survive the revocation window. The architecture described here makes the current applicable revocation state part of the final authorization predicate immediately before the consequence is committed.【294†¶】
L327: The architecture therefore targets revocation lag at the protected consequence boundary, including stale-token use, stale introspection, cached allow decisions, policy narrowing, multi-hop delegation, crash recovery, network partition, alternate effectuation paths, and races between revocation and commit.【295†¶】
L328: ## 【44†4.】 【45†Motivating Scenario: Valid at Issuance, Revoked Before Effectuation】
L329: 
L330: Consider a service or autonomous agent that prepares a consequential operation C. At time t0, principal A is authorized to perform C and a permit is issued. At t1, before C is externally effective, an authority disables A, revokes the grant, narrows the allowed destination set, or marks the relevant credential or workload as no longer acceptable.【296†¶】
L331: The revocation does not necessarily alter the bytes or signature of the already-issued permit. A verifier that considers only issuance-time facts can therefore accept a permit that is authentic but no longer applicable.【297†¶】
L332: The required property is not that every revocation must propagate instantaneously through every system. The required property is that the deployment explicitly defines the point at which revocation becomes authoritative for the protected consequence, and that an act cannot cross the protected commit after that point without satisfying the new state.【298†¶】
L333: ## 【46†5.】 【47†Problem Space】
L334: 
L335: ### 【48†5.1.】 【49†Revocation Is Not Expiry】
L336: 
L337: Short token lifetimes reduce exposure but do not eliminate the interval between a security-state change and expiry. A one-minute token can still be used fifty-nine seconds too long for a sufficiently consequential operation. Conversely, event-driven revocation can permit longer token lifetimes while maintaining stronger responsiveness.【299†¶】
L338: ### 【50†5.2.】 【51†Revocation Is Not an Authenticity Failure】
L339: 
L340: A revoked permit can remain cryptographically authentic. Signature verification establishes integrity and issuer authentication; it does not by itself establish that the authority represented by the signed object remains applicable now.【300†¶】
L341: ### 【52†5.3.】 【53†Revocation Notification Is Not Effectuation Enforcement】
L342: 
L343: A push event, stream update, revocation list, introspection response, cache invalidation, or policy update can communicate a revocation. The security property addressed here is achieved only when the consequence-bearing path cannot commit the protected effect after the revocation has become authoritative under the deployment's ordering rule.【301†¶】
L344: ### 【54†5.4.】 【55†Revoking a Token Is Not Always the Same as Revoking an Act】
L345: 
L346: A transaction can be derived from a token and then queued, delegated, translated, transformed, or handed to a downstream subsystem. Revoking the upstream token after that transformation may not automatically cancel the already-instantiated operation. High-consequence deployments therefore need to identify which pending acts are still revocable and where that revocation is enforced.【302†¶】
L347: ## 【56†6.】 【57†Threat Model and Assurance Scope】
L348: ### 【58†6.1.】 【59†Threat Severity and Applicability】
L349: This document does not assign one universal severity score because consequence varies by deployment. The threat deserves high attention where a stale authorization can cause an externally consequential or difficult-to-reverse effect, including transfer of funds, privilege or identity changes, release of sensitive data or model artifacts, cloud-control mutations, device actions, protected I/O, confidential-compute transitions, industrial operations, or other high-consequence state changes.【303†¶】
L350: The distinctive risk is that compromise or forgery is not required. A legitimate principal can hold a cryptographically valid, unexpired, correctly sender-constrained authorization that was valid at issuance but should no longer control the protected effect after an authoritative revocation, suspension, narrowing, ownership change, trust-state change, or superseding policy decision.【304†¶】
L351: For low-consequence operations, short token lifetimes or bounded revocation propagation may be an acceptable engineering tradeoff. For high-assurance operations, the deployment SHOULD explicitly identify the maximum acceptable revocation-staleness interval and the boundary at which stale authority is no longer permitted to cause the protected effect.【305†¶】
L352: ### 【60†6.2.】 【61†Adversary Capabilities】
L353: The adversary MAY control or compromise the requester, agent, application process, orchestration layer, ordinary host software, untrusted caches, or communication paths outside the protected enforcement boundary. The adversary MAY possess a legitimately issued authorization object and MAY have been legitimately authorized at an earlier time.
L354: The adversary MAY delay, replay, reorder, suppress, or selectively route revocation notifications; exploit cached introspection or policy decisions; restore snapshots; induce crash recovery; race an effect against a revocation; or seek an alternate path that does not consult current revocation state.【306†¶】
L355: The adversary is not required to forge a signature, steal another principal's token, defeat proof-of-possession, or break cryptography. The core attack succeeds if a previously valid authorization remains usable after the authoritative revocation point.【307†¶】
L356: ### 【62†6.3.】 【63†Baseline Revocation-Finality Profile】
L357: 
L358: In the baseline profile, the requester and network are untrusted. The revocation authority, the source of current revocation state, and the Finality Sink are trusted to follow the protocol. Cached or presented revocation state from the requester MUST NOT be treated as authoritative merely because the requester supplies it.【308†¶】
L359: ### 【64†6.4.】 【65†High-Assurance Revocation-Finality Profile】
L360: A higher-assurance deployment MAY additionally assume compromise of the general-purpose host operating system, application runtime, agent framework, policy-distribution cache, or orchestration software.
L368: ## 【70†7.】 【71†Design Goals and Non-Goals】
L369: 
L370: The primary goal is to bind the applicability of revocation to the moment at which a protected consequence becomes effective. A revocation that is authoritative before protected commit MUST be capable of preventing a still-pending Candidate Act from completing when that revocation applies to the act.【312†¶】
L371: This document does not define a universal identity system, universal revocation transport, universal policy language, new OAuth grant type, consensus protocol, blockchain, or globally synchronized clock. It also does not require every revocation to cancel every pending action. Deployments define the scope and semantics of revocation; the finality mechanism enforces those semantics at the protected boundary.【313†¶】
L372: The document does not claim to roll back a consequence that has already become externally effective. Where compensating transactions are possible, they are a separate application concern. Revocation finality is primarily prospective with respect to acts that remain non-effective.【314†¶】
L373: ## 【72†8.】 【73†Prevention and Mitigation Property】
L374: The architecture distinguishes prevention from mitigation. A deployment can claim the prevention property described here only for a protected consequence whose effectuation paths are completely mediated by an enforcement boundary that obtains authoritative revocation state and couples the final revocation decision atomically, or under an equivalent protected ordering rule, to the protected commit.【315†¶】

L389: 
L390: Where a deployment accepts cached status with bounded staleness, performs only periodic checks, leaves alternate paths outside the Finality Sink, or cannot serialize revocation against effectuation, the mechanism can still reduce exposure and shorten the stale-authority window, but that is mitigation rather than the same prevention guarantee.【317†¶】
L391: The architecture does not reverse a consequence that is already externally effective. Compensation, rollback of application state, recovery, and incident response remain separate concerns unless a particular application defines them as part of its protected commit model.【318†¶】
L392: ## 【74†9.】 【75†Existing Mechanisms and the Proposed Delta】
L393: 
L394: Existing mechanisms solve important parts of revocation and continuous authorization. This document is not premised on those mechanisms being absent or defective. The comparison below identifies the additional invariant being examined.【319†¶】
L395: ### 【76†9.1.】 【77†OAuth Revocation and Introspection】
L396: OAuth Token Revocation [【16†RFC7009】] defines a standardized way to revoke tokens. OAuth Token Introspection [【17†RFC7662】] allows a protected resource to query token activity and metadata. These mechanisms can directly satisfy the proposed invariant when the Resource Server is itself the complete, non-bypassable consequence boundary, obtains sufficiently current status, and couples that status decision to the protected effect.
L397: The proposed delta concerns deployments where authorization acceptance and consequence occur at different components or times, including queues, downstream services, device APIs, payment or storage commits, and other deferred effectuation paths.【320†¶】
L398: ### 【78†9.2.】 【79†Continuous Access and Externalized Policy】
L399: 
L400: Continuous-access systems and externalized policy engines can react rapidly to account, risk, policy, or entitlement changes. They are complementary inputs to this architecture. The proposed question is whether the resulting current decision remains load-bearing at the exact boundary where a pending act becomes externally effective, including after work has left the component that performed the earlier authorization check.【321†¶】
L401: ### 【80†9.3.】 【81†Attestation and Protected Compute】
L402: 
L403: RATS, EAT, confidential-computing, and hardware-rooted mechanisms can establish fresh trust evidence and protect enforcement state. The proposed delta is not a new attestation format; it is the binding of applicable revocation state to the final protected act and commit.【322†¶】

L1165: ### 【178†25.2.】 【179†Stale Introspection Result】
L1166: 
L1167: A resource cached an earlier active=true result. After revocation, the cached result remains inside its cache lifetime. Where current revocation is required, the sink rejects or refreshes state rather than equating cache freshness with current applicability.【422†¶】
L1232: ## 【216†33.】 【217†Required Classes of Test Vectors】
L1233: 
L1234: A concrete profile or implementation SHOULD test at least the following cases:【451†¶】
L1235:   * authorization and effect under the same revocation generation: succeed;【452†¶】
L1236:   * principal revoked before finalization: reject;【453†¶】
L1237:   * grant narrowed so the exact act is no longer permitted: reject;【454†¶】
L1238:   * unrelated revocation that does not apply to the act: succeed if policy says so;【455†¶】
L1239:   * stale but correctly signed permit after revocation: reject;【456†¶】
L1240:   * replayed old revocation state: reject;【457†¶】
L1241:   * lost or reordered revocation event: fail according to the defined continuity rule;【458†¶】
L1242:   * revocation and effect racing concurrently: produce the defined serialized result;【459†¶】
L1243:   * crash after status check but before effect: recover without reviving stale authority;【460†¶】
L1244:   * alternate effectuation path: demonstrate equivalent enforcement or identify the gap.【461†¶】
L1245: ## 【218†34.】 【219†Questions to the IETF Community】
L1246: 
L1247: Criticism, corrections, counterexamples, operational experience, prior-art pointers, and evidence that an existing IETF mechanism already provides an equivalent invariant are explicitly invited. Negative answers and recommendations to narrow the work are useful outcomes.【462†¶】
L1248:   1. Do existing OAuth revocation, introspection, transaction-token, or continuous-access patterns already guarantee that a revocation committed before a protected effect prevents that effect, including asynchronous or multi-hop cases?【463†¶】
L1249:   2. When a Resource Server accepts a request and hands work to a queue, database, payment rail, device API, or downstream workload, where should revocation stop being relevant and where should it remain load-bearing?【464†¶】
L1250:   3. Is a protected monotonic revocation generation useful as a common abstraction across token, workload, attestation, and application-policy systems, or is that abstraction too broad?【465†¶】
L1251:   4. Should revocation state be carried in the authorization object, re-established at the sink, or support both models?【466†¶】
L1252:   5. What ordering primitive is appropriate for the race between revocation and effectuation without requiring a globally synchronized clock?【467†¶】
L1308: ### 【252†38.7.】 【253†Partitions and Split-Brain】
L1309: 
L1310: Network partitions can create multiple apparently current revocation views. Deployments MUST define whether protected effects fail closed, use quorum/consensus, accept bounded staleness, or follow another explicit rule. An attacker MUST NOT be allowed to choose whichever stale partition yields authorization unless that is intentionally permitted.【504†¶】
L1311: ### 【254†38.8.】 【255†Non-Bypassability】
L1312: 
L1313: Every technical path capable of producing the protected consequence MUST preserve the revocation-finality invariant. Debug paths, recovery APIs, direct storage or device access, privileged host interfaces, and asynchronous workers require explicit review.【505†¶】
L1314: ### 【256†38.9.】 【257†Revocation-Status Privacy】
L1315: 
L1316: Revocation queries can reveal identity, employment status, account risk, service relationships, device trust, or operational timing. Implementations SHOULD minimize disclosure and SHOULD prefer scoped status answers, keyed commitments, privacy-preserving status structures, or local protected state where appropriate.【506†¶】
L1317: ### 【258†38.10.】 【259†Revocation as a Denial-of-Service Surface】
L1318: 
L1319: An attacker can attempt to forge, flood, or withhold revocation signals. Authentication and authorization of revocation events are required, and deployments SHOULD distinguish an authenticated revocation from simple status unavailability. Fail-closed semantics protect authorization but can reduce availability.【507†¶】
L1320: ### 【260†38.11.】 【261†Stale Introspection and Authorization Caches】
L1321: 
L1322: A cached active result, policy allow decision, or status response can outlive the revocation event that invalidates it. Implementations MUST define the maximum accepted staleness for each protected operation class. A cache entry whose freshness or generation cannot be established MUST NOT be treated as equivalent to authoritative current state in a profile that claims prevention.【508†¶】
